utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. Could the Registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And the appearances, for the parties.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian, Ann Sutherland, and Ruth Karper for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Well, Judge Schomburg is still ill and unable to come to court. For the same reason as stated yesterday, considering that there are still Defence witnesses in The Hague who are waiting to testify, it is in the interest of justice for Judge Argibay and I to continue sitting under Rule 15 bis to hear these remaining witnesses, even in the absence of Judge Schomburg. For the record, I would like again to ask that both parties and Dr. Stakic himself formally register their consent to this procedure for today's hearing, 13th March, year 2003. Starting with the Prosecution, Mr. Koumjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Prosecution consents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the Defence consents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And Dr. Stakic, do you have any objections?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. Therefore, considering that Judge Schomburg is still not available to sit in this case today because he continues to be ill, Judge Argibay and I, being satisfied that it is in the interest of justice to do so, and again, based on the consent of the parties and Dr. Stakic himself, hereby order pursuant to Rule 15 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, that for today, the hearing continue in the absence of Judge Schomburg. Well, there are just a few procedural matters to be dealt with before the witness is brought in. Firstly, the schedule for today and tomorrow. It is now confirmed that we will be able to sit tomorrow in Courtroom Number I from 5.00 to 7.00 p.m. And in this regard, I would like to thank you, Madam Registrar, and all participants for their efforts that made it possible for us to work tomorrow. There are two witnesses remaining for this week, Witness 043, who has been in The Hague since last week, and the expert witness, Srdja Trifkovic who apparently has some scheduling constraints. Mr. Lukic, is it your intention to conclude with the testimony of Witness 043 before starting with Mr. Trifkovic, or it will be necessary to interrupt Witness 043's testimony to accommodate Trifkovic's schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, our intention is to finish with the witness 043 first, and then to start with the testimony of the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. And the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: However the Defence wants to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Therefore, we shall continue hearing Witness 043 this afternoon, followed by Mr. Trifkovic. And we shall hopefully be in a position to sit tomorrow afternoon in order to finish the expert's testimony. As far as the next week witnesses are concerned, the Defence undertook to tell the Court by Thursday, that is today, the order of the witnesses for the next week. In order to assist the Defence, the Court in it's turn has ordered to call in addition to the military expert four witnesses for the next week. Mr. Lukic, do you have any additional information on the availability of the remaining witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We just contacted with the Victims and Witness Unit, and one of the newly proposed witnesses who is confirmed by the Chamber will be here hopefully on Monday. He should come to The Hague on Saturday, and we are trying to contact the priest who lives in the US. And concerning the Witness 058, we called his house this morning, but nobody was answering at that time. So our case manager is in the Defence room, and he is trying to contact this gentleman. So we have to admit that there is nothing final with this witness yet. And we hope that the Witness 089 will come the next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Did you contact him?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We spoke with him yesterday, and the problem is his health, as we informed the Court. He is diagnosed with leukemia, and he is under certain treatments which causes him to feel even more sick. But he will try to interrupt these medications and not to receive them the next week. In that case, he would be able to come to The Hague. Otherwise, he would probably not be able to travel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: So you are certain only about one witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Yes, the General and one witness. As to the rest, three witnesses, you have no reliable information and you are not sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Not yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: -- Whether they will come to The Hague or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We hope that we'll have until the end of today, this working day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Well, once more, I would like to ask you to inform us about the situation and about the availability of these witnesses. And let the Court know in which order they will come.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The new witness will testify on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: On Monday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then the General will testify on Thursday and Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Does the OTP have any comments on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No, except to say that we're -- we hope we can finish these two witnesses this week, but I don't think it's clear that we can. So it's possible we may have to finish one of these two witnesses in The Hague on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Well, let us try our best. Now I would like to remind the parties that the Registrar handed out a document entitled "problematic documents" to both parties last week indicating where there were still some problems or issues with various Prosecution and Defence exhibits. The Court would encourage the parties to try and resolve these issues as soon as possible. In this regard, I would like to say that yesterday, I omitted to admit the document that has been provisionally numbered Exhibit S406A/B into evidence. Are there any objections to admitting this document into evidence? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have any objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We move it into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Therefore, the document is admitted into evidence as Exhibit 406A/B respectively. Are there any other matters that the parties would like to raise at this moment? I have not seen any moves. Now we can continue with the evidence of Witness 043. Madam Registrar, can we please go into closed session for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Well, our next witness, or the next Defence witness, is Dr. Srdja Trifkovic. I take it that there is no protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: For this witness. Could the usher -- usher is working very efficiently. And for the record, Madam Registrar, I would like to take into account that on the part of the Defence, Joanna Korner is here with us. And case manager --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Danilo Cirkovic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, indeed I can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Could you please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. As Dr. Trifkovic is an expert witness appearing in the Defence case, Mr. Ostojic, please, the floor is yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Trifkovic. As you know, my name is John Ostojic, and along with Mr. Branko Lukic and our case manager, Danilo Cirkovic, we represent Dr. Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you a series of questions here today, if at any time, sir, you do not understand my question, please feel free to advise me and I will attempt to clarify the question so that you may understand it and give us a full and complete answer. Is that fair enough?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, for the record, can you give us your full name?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: My full name is Srdja Trifkovic. I sometimes go by the name of Serge, but my official name if Srdja Trifkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: For the purposes of a personal background, can you share with us your date of birth, place of birth?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: My date of birth is July 19th, 1954, in Belgrade, Serbia, as it was at time Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your current citizenship and residency?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I am a US citizen residing Highland Park, which is a suburb of Chicago in Illinois.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Defence has asked you, Dr. Trifkovic, to prepare a report Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. relating to the events leading up to and including the period of 1991 and 1992 in the Prijedor Municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm being asked, and I've frequently been asked this, to advise you, but mostly it's my fault, that we should attempt to make a pause between the question and answer since we both are speaking English, and the translators as well as our court reporters are unable sometimes to keep up, and we would hate to have anything overlap. So I would ask you, sir, to the extent possible that you pause before giving us your answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you prepare such a report giving us the background history as well as the events that preceded and included that during the Bosnian crisis and the Prijedor Municipality during the period of 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honours, that that report has been filed with the Court as well as tendered to the Office of the Prosecution. Do you have that report, Dr. Trifkovic, with you today?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I make it clear straight away there's no objection to this report being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Then Dr. Trifkovic's report be admitted into evidence -- excuse me. And if there is no objection on the either party, the expert report of Dr. Srdja Trifkovic filed in this case on the 3rd of March, year 2003, with the Registry, pages D14.754 through D14.804 is admitted as Exhibit D92A. For the record, the report is admitted in the English language only.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I may proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, within the report that we were just discussing that you captioned and title "Events in Prijedor, 1991, 1992, In the context of the Bosnian Crisis, A Background Report," that is indeed the title of your report. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Within that report, sir, you also attached your curriculum vitae as annex 1. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, just share with us your educational background, the degrees that you had attained and approximately when it is that you attained them.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I obtained my first BA degree in international relations at the University of Sussex in Great Britain in 1977. I obtained my second BA in political science at the University of Zagreb, Croatia, in 1987. And I obtained a Ph.D. in modern history at the University of Southampton in Great Britain in 1990. I also pursued post doctoral research at the Hoover Institution at Stanford University in California in 1991, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you share with us, Dr. Trifkovic, what languages you can speak?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Serbian is my mother tongue. I'm a native speaker. I also speak English and understand and use in my research French and German and Russian. I also have some limited conversational ability in Dutch, Italian, and Bulgarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, over the course of your career, have you ever been published?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If it helps, Mr. Ostojic, you can lead on all of this. There's no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It should just speed things up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, so extensively, that I would have to ask you to clarify whether you are referring to journalistic publications or refereed publications, i.e., scholarly quarterlies and books.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us exactly your work in the last 15 to 20 years with respect to any writings that you participated in or publications. Are all of them reflected in your annex 1 to your report that has been admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Frankly, no. What we have there is a select bibliography, and because so many articles, particularly as part of my regular work for chronicles, magazine, and other print publications remain unclassified that I frankly do not have the record of all of them. But all of the refereed publications, books, book chapters, and edited books have been quoted in my CV.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Tell us -- share with us --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel and witness please break between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us, Dr. Trifkovic, if you will your current employment and if you don't mind share with us your employment history.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: For most of my working life, I have combined a journalistic and an academic career. I started in journalism as a broadcaster with the BBC world service, with the Yugoslav service as it was then, back in 1980. During those six years at BBC, I moved also to the world service as a producer in what was, again at that time, talks and features department. And also in 1985, I worked as a subeditor in the world service newsroom. In 1986/7, I was for a year with the voice of America in Washington D.C. And thereafter, the southeast Europe correspondent based in Belgrade for the weekly magazine "US News" and "World Report," and also a stringer for the "Washington Times," which is a daily newspaper, during which time I was also associate editor of the Belgrade fortnightly magazine "Duga." After my year at the Hoover institution, in addition to my journalistic activities, I was also engaged in political consultancy with, among others, crowned Prince Alexander of Yugoslavia, Republika Srpska, the now former president of Yugoslavia Dr. Vojislav Kostunica, and a variety of private companies seeking to do business in that part of the world. In 1986/7, I was a visiting professor of international relations at the University of St. Thomas in Houston, Texas. In 1987 -- sorry, in 1996/7, correction. In 1997/98, I was at Rosehill College, South Carolina, and since the summer of 1998, foreign affairs editor of "Chronicles," which is a monthly magazine published by the RockFord Institute in Illinois. Within the institute since March of 2000, I have also been the director of the centre for international affairs. During this time, in addition to my regular monthly column for the magazine, and weekly world affairs commentary for the website, I have continued to publish for other publications, including related to the Balkans, the entry on the Bosnian war in the Almanac of World Politics published by the Oxford University Press in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me if I may just turn specifically to our case here. In preparation of your report, can you share with us what materials and sources you reviewed?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of my extensive experience and personal as well as professional interest in the wars of Yugoslav secession, the primary source was, of course, my accumulated and varied collection of experiences both concerning personal contacts and primary and secondary sources. But more specifically, I also read a number of articles from various Bosnian newspapers and magazines related more specifically to the situation in the area of Prijedor, most notably Kozarski Vjesnik, and a whole host of articles from the Sarajevo press, both daily and weekly, pertaining to the situation in 1991 and early 1992, as well as a number of academic studies, books published in the English language over the past few years, notably by people such as Bob Hayden, Paul Shoup, Susan Woodward and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Specifically to the best of your recollection, can you list the publications that you also reviewed other than Kozarski Vjesnik involving Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Prijedor Municipality or the events that transpired in 1991 and 1992 in the Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: I was supplied by a whole host of articles translated or not from Oslobodenje, from Darne, as well as book chapters by a number of former commanders of the Muslim forces in the early days, even before the war actually broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, is it true that you were also given a copy of the fourth amended indictment as it relates to Dr. Milomir Stakic?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, I actually printed it out from the ICTY website.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just for housekeeping matters, Your Honours, the materials that Dr. Trifkovic indeed -- and I ask that he verify it, include 65 ter exhibits that have not yet been admitted into evidence. And for our purposes now, if I may suggest, I'll just identify them. They are in a binder. They are Defence 65 ter exhibits 1 through 249, as well as 65 ter Defence exhibits 285, 287, and 288. And we would be asking if the Court wishes to have Dr. Trifkovic look at the three binders to his left to verify that those are the articles that he's reviewed, and then we would be moving to admit those into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Of course Dr. Trifkovic is welcome to look through these binders and exhibits, but it seems to me it's too much for a short observation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In the interests of time, I recognise that. I believe that we used a similar procedure with respect to Robert Donia. If necessary, we'll go through each one, we don't have a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, would you mind, to your immediate left, there are three binders, and if you could just take a quick perusal of the documents there and identify or verify for us whether you've actually reviewed those documents in connection with the preparation of your report that has been admitted into evidence here today.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Obviously the perusal has to be very quick, but short of a miraculous replacement of materials in the binders, I rest confident that these are the materials.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is there by any chance a list of what these documents are?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's a list that can be found on our 65 ter Defence submission of the 18th of November, 2002, which identifies by number the actual article as well as the title of the article, and subsequent to that the translation of the articles as was assisted by the unit translating them. Again, for the record the 65 ter numbers are 1 through 249, as well as Defence 65 ter number 285, 287, and 288.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the moment, we're not going to make complaint. But we were given this last week. We weren't told it had anything to do with this witness. And there's nothing to indicate in the witness's -- expert report that he ever looked at any document other than those he mentioned. So, Your Honour, for the moment I'll leave it until we have a look at it and see what they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Certainly I'd like to proceed but I don't want to debate the issue. I think his report clearly in the footnotes identify various sources including those that are included in the Defence 65 ter submissions, but we can address that at some other point I guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: We'll address this issue later on. Please do continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In addition, Dr. Trifkovic, to your personal experiences, your education, and your experience in the field of history, academic history and political science, and the materials that you've identified that you reviewed, did you also, sir, review a report by Robert Donia submitted by the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you also given, sir, Mr. Donia's testimony as it related to the Stakic case?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: What I reviewed was a long and a short version of Professor Donia's report. I did not review his oral testimony in the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And let us go right to the heart of the matter if we may. Can you describe the situation by way of background in the former Yugoslavia leading up to 1990 by starting with describing to us the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: After a period of economic and political liberalisation in the late 1960s, which was marked by an increase in investment activity and general prosperity, Yugoslavia was politically shaken by several events in the early 1970s. First of all, there was the nationalist awakening in Croatia, later known as "the Croat spring." Then there was Tito's day of reckoning, with economic liberalisers in Belgrade. And the 1974 constitution is the result of what in the political and economic sense was a retrenchment of the old party, political structures. The restatement of the commitment to the peculiar Titoist brand of Marxist Orthodoxy exemplified in socialist self management and the very cumbersome decision-making structure of both political and economic bodies, and perhaps most importantly, to our purposes, de facto confederalisation of the Yugoslav federation, including the granting to the two autonomous provinces within Serbia, Kosovo and Vojvodina, de facto status of republics by giving them seats on the collective presidency and -- both of the party and of the state, and giving them de facto veto powers that were enjoyed by other republics, too. All of this made some sense from the narrow party political viewpoint of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia, for as long as there was the ultimate arbiter in the person of Josip Broz Tito to mediate disputes and to legitimise both his personal autocratic rule and the one-party dictatorship of the League of Communists, albeit some would say that compared to other communist regimes, it was a velvety dictatorship, but dictatorship nevertheless. But with Tito's death in 1980, the ultimate arbiter was removed, and the whole edifice started grinding to a halt unlike some of the more responsible political leaders of the 20th century, and notably Francisco Franco Bahamonde, Tito belonged to those dictators who didn't particularly care what would happen after their departure from the scene. It is not only me, but many other Yugoslav commentators from different sides of the ethnic divide who may disagree about various other aspects of policy in the 1970s and the 1980s, but they all agree that Tito's attitude was comparable to Louis XV, "apres moi le deluge," after my deluge. Throughout the 1980s, the proof of this lamentable legacy of Titoism was best manifested in the inability of the system to reform itself from within. Because of the consensual decision-making structure that was mandated by the 1974 constitution, and at the same time, because of the widely differing levels of economic and cultural development and widely different interests and perceptions among the ethnic groups in the former Yugoslavia, it was well nigh impossible to make hard decisions about hard choices that faced the country and to overcome the accumulating problems both in the economic and the social and the political sphere that came to a head with the collapse of the Berlin wall and roughly a decade after Tito's death, resulted in the breakthrough of centrifugal forces that sought Yugoslavia's disintegration. One could say that throughout the 1980s, to come back to your question, thanks to the legacy of the 1974 constitution, in the institutional sense, and the legacy of Josip Broz Tito in the personal sense, Yugoslavia was on an automatic pilot to self-destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were there guarantees at that time for the different ethnic compositions or groups within the former Yugoslavia? And we're talking about the period immediately prior to 1990.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It should be remembered that the 1974 constitution was a strictly party political constitution that postulated the continued and open-ended existence and monopoly of power by the League of Communists and all of its subordinate bodies. So even though the constitution did provide a whole host of guarantees which in the case of minority rights and protections were quite detailed, sometimes ridiculously so, so that entering some multi-ethnic town in Vojvodina, you may see traffic signs in four or five different languages, nevertheless the crucial issue which concerned the right to self-determination was defined as residing with the constituent nations of Yugoslavia and not with the territorial administrative units comprising the Yugoslav federation. In addition, even the theoretical right to self-determination of the constituent nations, within the terms of that constitution, remained theoretical because the mechanism for the exercise of that right was not specified, and, at least by implication, was deemed unlikely to ever be exercised in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me understand historical, when did the Muslims become recognised as a constituent people in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The question is somewhat complex because throughout the history of the distinct ethnic group in Bosnia-Herzegovina that came into being from the members of the Islamised Slavic indigenous population, and to a much lesser extent, the newcomers from other parts of the Ottoman empire, under the Ottoman rule, there was no question of their classification as an ethnic group in its own right. They were bona fide citizens of the Uma, the Caliphate, the Ottoman empire. And by virtue of Islamic context, were fellow citizens of other Muslims wherever they may reside, whether it be in North Africa, Mesopotamia, or Anadolia. And the assumption was that a Slavic Muslim of Bosnia, by virtue of religious affiliation, had more in common with a fellow Muslim anywhere else in the Ottoman empire than with his Christian neighbour, orthodox or Catholic, doesn't matter, who spoke the same language and shared the same blood. After the Austrian occupation of 1878, an attempt was made by the viceroy of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Baron Benjamin von Kallay in the 1880s and 1890s to construct the Bosniak identity. And this experiment proved very appealing to the Muslims, but at least in theory, it was supposed to apply to all people who lived in Bosnia regardless of their denomination, regardless of their religion. The experiment did not prove long-lived, and it certainly did not affect Serbs and Croats who by that time certainly started feeling an integral part of the wider community of the Serbs to the east and the south, and the Croats to the west and the north.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt the doctor. But I wonder where you're going. Your Honours will recall that we were prevented from leading any evidence going prior to 1990 when Dr. Donia was called. Your Honour, the question was really a fairly simple, straightforward one. When did the Muslims become recognised as a constituent people in the former Yugoslavia. We've now gone all the way back to 1878. Your Honours, I don't mind. I understood that Dr. Trifkovic had to get away, and that he therefore wished to finish his evidence tomorrow. I have already indicated to Mr. Ostojic the length of time that I will require to cross-examine him. His report has gone in. If Mr. Ostojic, however, wishes to pursue this and wishes to take longer, then that's a matter for him. But then Dr. Trifkovic will be aware he will almost certainly have to remain on Monday or at least return at some later time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The answer is in 1961.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, I got your point. And really, the Bench advised the parties and the historian expert of the parties not to go deep in the history in order to save time. We are interested mainly in the recent history and in the events which help us to understand better what was going on in the former Yugoslavia since 1990, and especially in 1992. That's why I ask you to limit your questions to that period. And you, Dr. Trifkovic, to limit your answers to the relevant period established in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just make a point of comment, if we look at how long Dr. Donia took and purportedly that he confined his questions and answers to that period, I think the limited time that we're given, and we'll accept that limited time, and we understand the circumstances, but I certainly don't accept counsel standing up and objecting. The question was clear. There's no objection to the question. And we will attempt to move as quickly as possible. It was my not intention to go to the Ottoman empire. It is covered in the report. I'll confine my questions to that period of time. However, it's our view that in order to keep it in proper context, that it is necessary at times for Dr. Trifkovic to refer to the historical significance of various things such as the 1974 constitution, as well as when the Bosnian Muslims were considered a constituent nation within the former Yugoslavia in order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Sure, but I ask, and I advised you, to be as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'm trying my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think, Dr. Trifkovic, you told us 1961. Briefly, with respect to that date, prior to 1951, my last question I trust on the prior period, were the Muslims of the former Yugoslavia a constituent nation?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The point I was trying to make earlier is that 1961 was the cutoff point when they came Muslims with a capital "M" to use the parlance of Tito's Yugoslavia from the time. But they were certainly treated as Yugoslavs, ethnically not committed or nondeclared. And the point I was trying to make is that their proclamation as a nation that carried a confessional adjective carried a lot of semantic confusion, and that that semantic confusion could have been avoided if previous rulers of Bosnia been more careful and more mindful of the implications of the attachment of a strictly confessional label to the name of an ethnic group. I'm aware that we don't have time to dwell on this in detail, but at the same time I think it's important to bear in mind that what happened in 1961 with this formal designation was an act of communist volunteerism par excellence. No reasonable person would deny that the Muslims as they were known from that time on were an ethnic group in their own right with their mentality, with their historical memories, with their political interests. But that the choice of the Titoist establishment in the selection of the term was most unfortunate.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Directly, let me ask you this: Since 1938, when was the first multiparty elections in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What led to the November 1990 elections?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The collapse of the League of Communists of Yugoslavia that had been on the cards for some years previously, but became fully apparent at the 15th congress of the LCY in January of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Again, being reminded to pause. I'll attempt to do so. What if anything was the significance of the November 1990 elections and why?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The significance was that the three ethnically-based parties, the SDA, the HDZ/BH, and the SDS created a coalition in order to defeat the renamed and formally restructured League of Communists. It is indeed counterintuitive, but it makes a lot of sense, as I tried to point out in my report, that the three parties that were very different in their self-perception and their views of the future nevertheless entered a tactical electoral alliance in order to get rid of the old lot and turn an altogether new leaf. So what we had after the November election was a tripartite coalition that entered into power-sharing arrangements at all levels, both the government in Sarajevo and the municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We're maybe getting a little quicker than I needed at this moment. Were there other parties, political parties, that sought office other than the three ethnic parties that you described? And if I may just -- can you tell us what those three ethnically-based parties are and tell us whether there were other parties that existed at that time.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The three ethnically-based parties were the SDA,, the Party of Democratic Action; the Croatian democratic alliance of Bosnia-Herzegovina, HDZ/BH; and the Serbian democratic party, SDS. We also had the renamed communists led by Nijaz Durakovic, and we had the League of Communists movement for Yugoslavia. It was a more doctrinaire party that claimed the legacy of Titoism and was mainly supported by Partizan veterans and YPA personnel. We had the alliance of reform forces led by then federal Prime Minister Ante Markovic. And we had a whole array of smaller parties, most of which did not obtain electoral -- rather parliamentary representation. In fact, except for the ones that I've mentioned, I cannot recall others that got into the assembly at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, the result of the elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina and former Yugoslavia in November of 1990 resulted in a new power structure, as you mentioned, three party coalition. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Share with us how it worked and for how long it worked.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: In the early months, it worked surprisingly well. In fact, the proponents of the old regime were making very scary predictions about the suggested inability of what they called nationalist parties to work together. But in the period from November of 1990 until roughly the summer of 1991, maybe for over half a year, the distribution of posts at different levels proceeded relatively smoothly with a Muslim becoming president of the collective presidency, a Croat becoming the prime minister, and a Serb, the speaker of the assembly. And this pattern was replicated through local agreements at the municipal level between the three parties, depending on the ethnic composition of a given locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When if at all did the tripartite coalition begin to have -- experience problems and why?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: There is no cutoff date, but with the declaration of independence by Croatia and Slovenia and the rising violence in Croatia, it became obvious that the six-republic Yugoslavia as it had existed between 1945 and that time was no longer viable. With the prospect of the secession of two republics, Croatia and Slovenia, the Muslim leadership increasingly started talking of their intention to secede from rump Yugoslavia, of their refusal to remain in the reduced Yugoslavia of four republics, and the Serbs equally assertively talked of their determination not to be taken out of the Yugoslav framework against their will. So I would suggest that the symptoms of the breakdown in the summer of 1991 were external to Bosnia-Herzegovina in that the divergent views of the future were contingent upon the developments, primarily in Croatia - Slovenia doesn't really come into this - developments over which the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina had very little control. In addition, the Tudjman regime in Zagreb had a vested interest in fanning the embers of conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because at that time creating a tactical alliance with the Muslims, who he otherwise disliked and despised, was an exercise as far as he was concerned as politics of the art of the possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You mentioned, sir, the inner party agreement and the posts that were initially obtained following the November 1990 elections. Can you tell us to the extent that you know how many levels of government there were post-November 1990?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: There was the republic, there were the regions, and there were municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So those three forms of government existed, and people were essentially elected to each of those posts. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Except for the regions where the nominations were based on the already-elected bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for us in a little more detail how the interparty agreement worked and whether or not it worked on all three levels of government, namely, the republic, regional, and municipal levels.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The first symptoms of serious tension in the functioning of the agreement occurred in the summer of 1991 in relation to the distribution of posts within the Ministry of the Interior, MUP. It is only with hindsight that we know the extent to which the SDA activists had started preparing for the possibility of armed conflict several months before this tension became apparent, and it is only with hindsight, with the knowledge that we have today, that we can fully understand the reasons that guided the SDA-led Ministry of the Interior to risk the breakdown of the agreement, or at least the tensions within its application, for the sake of controlling the mechanism of the interior ministry both in the centre, in Sarajevo, and to the greatest possible extent at the level of municipalities. But nevertheless, in answer to your question, the real breakdown occurs in October of 1991, specifically on the night of October 14th, 15th, when the Croat and Muslim deputies in the middle of the night and without Serb deputies being in attendance adopted the memorandum on independent and sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that in a moment, Doctor. Let me just if, I may focus, the question on the following, with the Court's permission: Do you know what the chamber of equality of nations is and how does it play a role in Bosnia-Herzegovina and specifically the effect it may have on the Prijedor Municipality in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The chamber that you mention never came into being. And I stand corrected: This was another reason for the tensions in the summer of 1991. It was a body that was envisaged under the amendments to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina enacted in the summer of 1990, amendments, by the way, that paved the way to the multiparty elections four months later. Under those amendments, a separate chamber was supposed to be created within the Bosnia-Herzegovinian assembly that would be composed of equal numbers of Serb, Croat, and Muslim deputies. I believe there were supposed to be 20 of each, but I would need to check this. And that any decision dealing with the constitutional issues and legal issues that may affect the rights of the constituent nations of Bosnia-Herzegovina could be referred to this body by at least 20 deputies in the chamber of citizens in the BH assembly, and that only with the agreement of this chamber and with the acceptance of the proposed legislation by the representatives of all three constituent nations would it be possible to take the draft back to the assembly for further debate and eventual vote. This was really supposed to be an insurance policy for Bosnia-Herzegovina's constituent nations against the possibility of two ganging up against one. Oddly enough, in the summer of 1990, there were some Muslims who believed that this body could also offer them a modicum of protection against the possibility of Serbs and Croats getting together in order to engineer some kind of split or partition. But in the event, by 1991, a tactical alliance was in the making between Croats and Muslims for different reasons. We may get into those later on. And they refused to proceed with the establishment of this Chamber which was a source of endless complaints and deep mistrust on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Immediately prior to the war in Croatia, was Bosnia-Herzegovina part of what was considered at that time the former Yugoslavia, as a republic state?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: It most certainly was.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And during that time, as a member of the former Yugoslavia, it being a republic state, was there a decision made by any political parties as to what position should be taken in a conflict by a seceding former republic, namely Croatia?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: There was a great deal of ambiguity, and one might even say duplicity on the part of the SDA. On the one hand, many public statements were made to the effect that the Muslims would remain impartial and neutral in the Serb/Croat dispute that by the summer of 1991 escalated into a shooting war in Croatia. On the other hand, however, as early as March 1991, political decisions were made to start creating a paramilitary Muslim militia, and even before the first shots were fired in Croatia, in early June of 1991, this was given full political imprimatur of the top SDA leadership. By June of 1991, with the secession of Croatia and Slovenia clearly on the agenda, Izetbegovic's view was fairly faithfully reflected in his memorable statement that he would be prepared to sacrifice peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina for the sake of independence, sovereignty, but he would not be prepared to sacrifice independence for the sake of peace. As far as the SDS was concerned, it's posture was throughout this period largely reactive, which reflected its essentially -- essential preference for the status quo, i.e., Bosnia-Herzegovina should remain within Yugoslavia, any Yugoslavia. And as far as the HDZ is concerned, they were hardly an autonomous body within Bosnia-Herzegovina, to all practical intents and purposes, their policy was created in Zagreb. And their view was that they would pay lip service to Bosnia's independence and territorial integrity as the first step to what they themselves and everybody else knew was their long-term objective, which is either to attach the whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina to a Greater Croatia, or else to have a de facto annexation of the majority Croat areas of western Herzegovina and the Sava River valley to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, you mentioned approximately 25 minutes or so ago the memorandum on sovereignty. Can you tell us when that was passed and the circumstances surrounding its ultimate implementation.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The memorandum was the subject of a heated debate in the four days preceding the illegal vote on the night of October 14/15th, and it was prompted by the involvement of what goes under the name of the international community, and was primarily at that time limited to what until the end of 1991 was the European Community.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Doctor, I apologise to interrupt. But when you say October 14th and 15th, that is also of 1991. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The Serb deputies claimed that the assembly was not authorised to put this issue to the vote without the agreement and the participation of the Serbs, and when the debate was adjourned on the evening of October 14th, Serbian deputies simply left assuming that this was the end of the proceedings for the day. But Croats and Muslims were surreptitiously informed to reconvene, one might say, conspiratorially and in the middle of the night and to carry the vote by simple majority. I am not a constitutional lawyer, and so I can only limit my comments on this particular episode to the opinion of people who are, such as Robert Hayden, who has no doubt that this move was both illegal and illegitimate. What I can say is that in political terms, it was tantamount to throwing a gauntlet to the Serbs effectively telling them that the principle of consensual decision-making is out, that the principle of simple majority rule is in, and that an effectively revolutionary act was performed on that night with which they will have to live whether they wanted it or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the Court wants me to proceed now or if there's any...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, there was an issue in our case specifically relating to a referendum that was ultimately called for in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you tell us about that. When it was, how it came into being, and why was it called?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The referendum was the direct consequence of the encouragement given by the Badinter commission created by the European Union to the republics of the former Yugoslavia to apply for recognition and the deadline of January 15th was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of 1992. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The Badinter commission further postulated two things, one that because the will of the people of Bosnia-Herzegovina had not been clearly expressed, this verification ought to be done by the means of a referendum. And secondly, that in future arrangements, and I quote from memory: "Minority rights of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina would have to be respected." Now, this was a doubly alarming development as far as the Serbs were concerned because in Croatia it was already decided by the Tudjman regime that they would be denied the status of a constituent nation under the Croatian constitution. Let us remember that both in Croatia and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbs were, in the case of Croatia, one of two; in the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, one of three constituent nations. Suddenly in Croatia, they faced the situation of being reduced to the level of an ethnic minority overnight. And in the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the proposed rules of the Badinter commission, and also the substance of a referendum threatened to do the same, i.e., in constitutional terms, they lose the status of a constituent nation and they lose the right to consensual decision-making on issues of vital importance to the future of the three constituent nations and of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a whole. In practical terms, the referendum, which is an inherently unsuitable mechanism for ethnically mixed environments was suggested because it was clearly the mechanism which, if based on the simply majority of 50 per cent plus 1, as Izetbegovic interpreted it to mean, meant the exclusion of one whole group. In this particular case, the Serbs, but because of the peculiar arithmetics of the Bosnian situation, that could have also meant Serbs plus Croats versus Muslims deciding in a referendum to carve Bosnia up and disintegrate it or Serbs and Muslims outvoting the Croats and deciding to remain part of Yugoslavia. Either way, referenda are taken by constitutional scholars to be appropriate, especially in simple majority is required, only in monoethnic environments to decide on issues such as in the case of Italy in 1947 whether it would be a republic or a monarchy and so on. The referendum on Bosnia's sovereignty and independence on February 29th and March the 1st was no more than a population census. And its inherent illegality and illegitimacy was compounded by the fact that only 62 per cent of registered voters turned up, and 61 point some voted in favour, which means that even in terms of the accepted principle of established democracies, that two-thirds majority would be required to alter constitutional arrangements was also disregarded, all of which provided us with the fuel for raised expectations on one side and the dark foreboding of the denial of all rights and the interest in these proceedings on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Shall I proceed? Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What was the SDS, and the Serb, the ethnic Serbs reaction, to the referendum of February 29, March 1st, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: There was no immediate reaction, because at that time, negotiations were preceding under the auspices of the Portuguese diplomat Cutileiro who was working closely with the EU chief negotiator Lord Peter Carrington, that sought to rearrange Bosnia-Herzegovina into a de facto federation of three ethnically-based cantonal units. The Serbs were prepared to contemplate the possibility of Bosnia-Herzegovina's independence, provided that this was accompanied by international guarantees that internal rearrangement of its constitutional principles on the basis of three ethnically-based units would be supported by the EC or EU, and accepted by the other two parties. In the event it was accepted by the HDZ but rejected by the SDA [Realtime transcript read in error "SDS"], for reasons that would probably need more detailed elaboration than the time allows us now, and the result was, I believe, on 28th of March, the walkout of Serb deputies from the joint assembly which was preceded, of course, on the 9th of January, 1991, with the creation of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which in itself was the reaction to the SDA/HDZ request for EU recognition. I'm afraid with this question, we moved -- we jumped across several other intermediary stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and we'll address those. Dr. Trifkovic, before you is a monitor, and specifically on page 79, line 10, it states that "this was rejected by the SDS." I believe your testimony was that this was rejected by the SDA.

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So it's just a mistake in terms of what they heard or how you may have said it. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, what was the position of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: The position of the SDS in the aftermath of what we can now call the historic night of October 14th/15th was that the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina will not be taken out of Yugoslavia by force and will not be prevented from exercising its legal and constitutional rights as guaranteed both by the Serbian and -- sorry, the Yugoslav and the Bosnia-Herzegovinian constitution. An immediate reaction took the form of the plebiscite of the Serb people in Bosnia-Herzegovina on November 8th, but it is important to remember that the plebiscite, unlike the referendum, did not represent an attempt to undermine the Bosnia-Herzegovinian political and constitutional framework; it had the character more of a declaratory and symbolic collection of the will of the Serbs in the republic. Likewise, the proclamation of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina on January 9th of 1992 was a reactive move, reactive to the stated intent of European Community to recognise Bosnia and the stated intent of the SDA/HDZ coalition to seek that recognition. And it still by virtue of postulating the Bosnia-Herzegovinian framework did not seek the separation of the Serbian political entity from the BH framework. That, in actual fact, came later in the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me -- if I just may interrupt and clarify two points in our historical continuum. When you say that the memorandum of sovereignty was October 14th and 15th of 1991, the reaction or the response by the Serbs, namely the SDS, was this plebiscite on November 8th of 1991. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: Correct, except that it wasn't just an SDS plebiscite. Other political groups, some of them hitherto opposed to the SDS as well as other nationalist parties as they called them, came out in favour of Yugoslav framework, notably the League of Communists movement for Yugoslavia, and a host of influential social and political organisations such as the veterans' association, Savez Borez [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, explain to me, if you can, the formation and proclamation of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that was a response to what exactly? Why did the Serbs form their own republic on the 9th of January, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SRDJA TRIFKOVIC
utterances.text: That was the response to the deadline for the request for recognition of Yugoslavia's former republics which was the 15th of January of 1992 and the declared intention of the rump presidency and the rump leadership in Sarajevo, "rump" meaning the SDA/HDZ coalition, to seek that recognition. Having ascertained that their protests and their demands for the respect of constitutionality and legality were in vain, the Serbian leaders opted for what one might term extra constitutional course, but ever after October 14th, everybody was acting extra constitutionally and extra legally. So whereas in isolation, that act did not have its basis in the 1974 constitution or the 1990 amendments, it is impossible to look at it in isolation from the developments that had preceded had. And most notably, the decision by the rump BH assembly to act illegally and unconstitutionally three weeks previously. I'm talking about the plebiscite. To act illegally and unconstitutionally starting with the night of October 14th, 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Before we conclude, I would like to tell the parties that Madam Registrar informed me that we could sit from 1600 [Realtime transcript read in error "1400"] to 1800 hours in Courtroom III tomorrow instead of 1700 to 1900 hours in Courtroom I. In this regard, may I ask Madam Registrar will it be possible to sit an extra hour in Room I from 18 to 19?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: First of all, it's from 16 hours to 18 hours, and not from 14 to 18. Regarding a third hour of hearing, so far I don't think it's possible. I will again double check, but I wouldn't count on this third hour for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Okay. Then what will be of option of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we better raise this. I don't know. Dr. Trifkovic as I understood it was due to testify Wednesday. It was then put back until Thursday. I'm told by Mr. Ostojic that Dr. Trifkovic cannot be here after tomorrow. He will not be concluded at the rate we're going in chief. I don't know even know that we're going to finish in chief tomorrow by the rate we're going. But he certainly -- cross won't be concluded in two hours tomorrow. So it's up to Your Honours to either order Dr. Trifkovic to come back on Monday or whatever is the appropriate solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm just merely waiting for my -- yes. Thank you. Your Honour, Dr. Trifkovic, we believe, is obviously an important witness for the Defence. And in the entire historical and political perspective offered here. Another solution may be is that we request, as opposed to order, Dr. Trifkovic to come the week after the 21st, which I understand his schedule may permit. However, we know and understand, and we are committed to concluding this case on the 21st of March as ordered and agreed to by the parties. I don't necessarily and would not like to impose an order on Dr. Trifkovic. And I committed personally to him that he would be complete this week. Some of this is obviously outside our control in light of the prior two witnesses that we had. But I would accept any suggestion the Court has, and perhaps we can ask Dr. Trifkovic himself since we are no longer able to have contact with him what exactly his schedule is and how he can assist us in that vein.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On Thursday on Friday next week, I have long-scheduled lectures at Queen's University in Kingston, Ontario, and the University of Toronto which if cancelled, and they had been advertised in advance, and will not be catastrophe, of course, but would create embarrassment and inconvenience. So I don't know if you will indeed conclude the proceedings by the 21st, if there is any possibility of this not being so, I would be happy to re-present myself on Monday --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm not quite clear, what's wrong with next Monday is the lecture is the end of next week. What is wrong -- Monday is, in fact, the 17th of March. And if the lecture is at the end, certainly Dr. Trifkovic won't go beyond the Monday, provided I get the amount of time that I told Mr. Ostojic I need.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I didn't emphasise is that I, as it happens, have to earn my daily bread, and that my absence from my day job which is at the "Chronicles" magazine at the Rockford Institute which has already been somewhat reluctantly accepted by my editor will request my presence for the conclusion of the May issue of the magazine and the editing of the website. I know that these are mundane personal issues that may be of no particular relevance to the Court. But they matter a great deal to me personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: But, Dr. Trifkovic, you know, you were informed beforehand about your testimony before the Tribunal. And the Bench hoped that the Defence explain you the specifics of testimony before the Court and the delays that are possible. So you had to reserve some extra time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly did do that because I came on Tuesday morning. And I was told that the three full days, Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday, would be more than ample. I actually spent a whole day Tuesday and whole day yesterday and most of the day today just waiting for this moment to come. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I understand your difficulties. But the Defence had to organise the order and the time of witnesses in a more proper way.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I have any choice in the matter, I would rather be back in Rockford to complete the issue of the magazine on Tuesday and Wednesday, and cancel my lectures and fly back rather than stay until Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: With all due respect to the Court, we were ordered, and we tried painstakingly through the court officer to explain the situation with the witnesses. But the Court called two judicial witnesses, specifically. And it was our understanding that those witnesses would take no longer than a day. And it transpired the first witness took far longer which we anticipated. The second witness also took far longer than it should have. And I understand the Defence brought the witness in anticipation that he would testify. We obviously didn't anticipate the Court maintenance for this Friday because we haven't had one in several months. And previously when I spoke to Dr. Trifkovic in February and prior to that, it was these three days that we scheduled him for. We believe that the two options that are available are the one that Dr. Trifkovic suggests, coming later in the week next week, although I have to check with my other witness. The Court in its discretion may open the deadline of March 21st so that Dr. Trifkovic can come back on March 24th to conclude his testimony. That's certainly up to the Court to make that decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Let us explore the possibility to have Dr. Trifkovic's testimony next week. Let us think about that. And tomorrow we come again to this question -- to this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do have one other question if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Dr. Trifkovic, until your testimony here is concluded, you may not contact the representatives of either the Defence or the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: Please be back tomorrow at -- we agreed, yes, at 1600 hours to continue with your evidence in this case. You're excused.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: And one last question to the Defence. Mr. Lukic, do you have any new information on the Defence witnesses for the next week?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First of all, we contacted the Witness 089. And now it's definite that he is not going to come the next week. We could not convince him because of his illness, and we didn't have a right to try to endanger his health. Regarding the other witness, 058, who was also examined by a doctor today. We couldn't find him. So hopefully, we'll try tonight, and we'll have the definite answer tomorrow whether he's able to come or not. Also due to his sickness. And to be able to schedule Dr. Trifkovic, we would like to know whether this trial would be finalised on the 21st or, as we heard some rumours, that it might be prolonged in the week of 24th with the Trial Chamber witness. So if that week would be open, maybe we can put Dr. Trifkovic in that week. If not, we'll then have to deal only with the next week. And in that case, maybe we could ask Dr. Trifkovic to consent to testify the next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: I have heard any [sic] rumours. So let us return to this issue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: The trial stays adjourn until tomorrow, 4.00 p.m., Courtroom Number III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VASSYLENKO
utterances.text: at 7.23 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 14th day of March, 2003, at 4.00 p.m. 21 22 23 24 25
